newsitem.title: UK: Stakis targets 7.5 pct hotel room rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Stakis targets 7.5 pct hotel room rate rise.

text.p: Scottish-based hotel and casino group Stakis Plc expects to achieve an increase of 7.5 percent on average for the year in its hotel room rates and an occupancy level of 76 percent, said chief executive David Michels in an interview.

"In the first quarter we did 10 percent, but I still think the average will be 7.5 percent or more over the year," said Michels. "Our forecast is to finish this year at 76 percent occupancy," he said.

Earlier Stakis reported an increase in its average room rate to 50.10 pounds in the first 13 weeks of 1997 up from 45.58 pounds. Occupancy levels fell to 71.8 percent over the same period from 72 percent in the first quarter of 1996.
"In real terms we are just back to where room rates were in the late 1980s. Room rates have just about reached their pre-recession levels in the provinces," said Michels.
Although January has been a typically dull month for hotel occupancy future bookings are at similar levels to last year, giving every confidence that Stakis can achieve the target, said Michel.

"January is always a miserable month and it has not disappointed in hotels, but after January it looks healthy," he said. He expects Stakis casinos to show a similar performance in the second quarter to the first.
Attendance at Stakis 23 casinos rose to 603,000 in the first quarter from 525,000 but spend per head fell to 110 stg over the same period from 129 stg.
The fall in spend per head mainly reflected the sale of the Barracuda casino in April last year to Ladbrokes, said Michel. The spend per head at the Barracuda averaged 450 pounds.
But Michel was encouraged by the increased casino attendance. "More people realise that they are a reasonable night out, you don't have to spend 100 pounds," he said.
"We have spent a year trying to make them do so, we've made a number of conversions, one big new build, and promotions to our base membership of 900,000, and we have introduced new training tables."
The improvements have coincided with an increase in newspaper and television interest in casinos.
